title: Neuron top-1 matches against J-lens vectors, without SAEs
takeaway: Classifying every MLP neuron by whether its single strongest weight alignment falls among the J-lens vectors at that layer or among an equal-sized pool of neuron directions from neighbouring layers, the J-lens share rises from roughly 15% below the workspace band to 60-65% inside it, against a 50% chance line. The measurement reaches the same conclusion as the SAE-based breadth analysis without depending on sparse autoencoders at all.
walkthrough:
Figure 77 is a per-layer curve. The horizontal axis is depth, in the paper's convention of 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed to the range 0-100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). The vertical axis is a fraction of MLP neurons. A dashed horizontal line marks 50%.

The classification behind that fraction runs as follows. Every neuron in an [[mlp-block]] has an input weight row, which reads from the [[residual-stream]], and an output weight column, which writes back to it. Each weight vector is compared by [[cosine-similarity]] against two pools of directions. The first pool is the [[jacobian-lens]] vectors at that layer, the directions along which the model encodes its potential to verbalize a token. The second is an equal-sized sample of neuron weight directions drawn from adjacent layers. The neuron is assigned to whichever pool holds its single strongest match.

Because the two pools are the same size, a neuron with no preference falls in either with probability one half. That is what the dashed line at 50% represents.

The two-pool design exists because raw cosines are noisy. The residual stream carries far more feature directions than it has dimensions ([[superposition]]), so a weight vector has appreciable cosine with directions it has no functional relationship to. A top-1 match counts as evidence only against a matched alternative.

What the curve shows: the share of neurons whose top match is a J-lens vector sits at roughly 15% before the workspace layer range and rises to 60-65% within it ([[workspace-layers]]). Below the workspace the neurons prefer their neighbours' weight directions; inside it, a clear majority point at the [[j-space]] instead.

This is the same breadth test as Figure 76 with the sparse-autoencoder machinery removed ([[neuron-connectivity]]). Figure 76 sorted [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions into six strata by lens kurtosis ([[lens-kurtosis]]) and asked which stratum each neuron matched; Figure 77 drops that dictionary and uses J-lens vectors directly.

The corroboration matters for the depth-broadcast claim. Figure 32 measured [[mlp-gain]], running directions through the MLP and finding J-lens vectors amplified about tenfold in the workspace band. Figure 77 reaches a compatible conclusion from static weights alone ([[j-space-broadcast]]). The paper reports one range for this variant in prose and does not separate the read side from the write side, as Figure 76 does.

terms.definition: A single unit inside a transformer's feed-forward block: one row of the block's input matrix that reads a direction from the residual stream, and one column of its output matrix that writes a direction back. Every neuron in the layer is classified once here.
The weight row a neuron uses to read from the residual stream. Its alignment with a pool of directions says which representations the neuron is positioned to pick up.
The weight column a neuron uses to write back into the residual stream. Its alignment says which representations the neuron is positioned to contribute to.

For one neuron weight vector, the single direction out of all candidates with which it has the highest cosine similarity. The neuron is labelled by whichever pool that one direction came from, so each neuron contributes exactly one vote.
The scale-free alignment measure used for every comparison in the figure: the cosine of the angle between a neuron's weight vector and a candidate direction.

The per-token directions produced by the paper's Jacobian lens, each encoding the model's potential to verbalize one vocabulary token. Here they form one of the two candidate pools a neuron's weights are matched against.

The region of representation space spanned sparsely by the J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as the model's global workspace. A neuron whose top match is a J-lens vector is counted as pointing at the J-space.

The control pool: neuron weight directions taken from layers next to the one under test. They are directions the model actually uses, so the comparison is against real internal structure rather than random noise.
The control pool is drawn to the same size as the J-lens pool. Matching the sizes is what makes the null 50%, since a larger pool would win top-1 matches simply by having more candidates in it.
The horizontal reference line in the plot. It marks the fraction expected if neurons had no preference between the two equal-sized pools.
Depth in the model, reported on the paper's rescaled index: 25 evenly spaced layers renumbered 0 to 100 so the number reads as a percentage of total depth.
The share of that layer's MLP neurons whose top-1 match landed in the J-lens pool. The two pools' shares sum to 1, so one curve determines the other.

The middle band of depth in which the paper finds the J-space behaving like a workspace, roughly after the first third of layers and before the final few. The rise in this figure is located relative to that band.

The paper's name for this family of tests: for each neuron, ask which population its strongest match falls in. It measures how widely J-space directions connect to neurons, as opposed to how strongly.
Sparse autoencoder decoder directions, the dictionary of sparsely active feature directions used as the candidate pool in Figure 76. This figure is the variant that removes them.
The statistic Figure 76 used to grade SAE features by how sharply their J-lens readout peaks on a few tokens, and so how far they lie in the J-space. It plays no part in Figure 77.
The running per-position vector that MLP neurons read from and write to. All the weight directions compared here live in its coordinate space.

The hypothesis that the residual stream packs more feature directions than it has dimensions. It is the reason a neuron has non-trivial cosine with directions it is unrelated to, and hence the reason a matched control pool is needed.
The measurement in Figure 32 that this figure corroborates: the output norm of the next MLP block applied to a unit direction, normalized so random directions score 1.
The claim under test: that the model's weights are arranged to distribute J-space content to many downstream components, here along the layer axis via MLPs.
The model the paper reports on by default, and so the model these neuron counts come from unless stated otherwise.

numbers.meaning: The dashed chance line. Two candidate pools of equal size means a neuron with no preference lands in the J-lens pool half the time, so 50% is the null this figure is read against.

The share of neurons whose top-1 match is a J-lens vector at layers before the workspace range. It is well below the 50% null, so in the sensory band neurons are preferentially aligned with neighbouring-layer neuron directions rather than with the J-space.

The share of neurons whose top-1 match is a J-lens vector inside the workspace layer range. A clear majority, and roughly a fourfold increase over the pre-workspace share, which the paper reads as MLP neurons being disproportionately wired to J-space-aligned directions where the workspace is active.
Only the single strongest match per neuron is counted. Using one match rather than a threshold is what makes the test robust to the overall noise level in cosines.
The J-lens vectors at the layer, and the adjacent-layer neuron directions. Two pools rather than the six of Figure 76 is why the null moves from 1/6 to 1/2.
The null in Figure 76, where each neuron chose among six equal-sized SAE strata. Quoted here only to explain why the dashed line differs between the two figures.

Figure 76's read-side peak: in the early workspace layers the top-kurtosis SAE stratum claimed up to 42% of neurons against 6% for the bottom stratum, both against the 1/6 null. These are the SAE-based numbers Figure 77 is meant to corroborate without SAEs.
The size of each of the six SAE strata in Figure 76. The paper does not state the pool size used for the two pools in Figure 77, only that they are equal to each other.
The kurtosis-percentile bins of Figure 76. Figure 77 replaces this whole graded ladder with a single two-way choice.
The reporting convention for the horizontal axis. Results are computed on 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers and renumbered so that positions read as percentages of depth.
The peak MLP gain of J-lens vectors in Figure 32, against a gain near 1 for neuron output directions. That functional result is the one this weight-level figure corroborates.

numbers.value: roughly the first third of depth
numbers.meaning: The sensory band, where the J-space carries essentially no meaningful content. The 15% regime in this figure sits in and just after that band, and the rise begins near its end.
